prompt: Close-up of one chilled layered dessert in a small, plain, straight-sided clear glass tumbler, one quarter of the recipe. Through the glass: two layers of soft, moist, spongy ladyfinger pieces, roughly 4–6 cm long, patchy light to medium coffee-brown, with darker soaked surfaces and pale golden-beige porous centres. Between and above them, two thick layers of pale ivory-yellow cream, airy and creamy yet softly set, with a few tiny soft mascarpone lumps and a gently levelled, unpiped top. Fine, dry, matte, deep cocoa-brown powder forms a continuous, slightly uneven dusting. No steam. The dessert fills 80% of the square frame; camera 45° above, textures sharp, rim and a narrow neutral table strip softly blurred. Warm soft natural side light, 85 mm lens, f/5.6, true-to-life colours, professional magazine food photo. Clean rim; no garnish, props, text, logos, hands or people.

visible_ingredients.real_life_appearance: The raw yolks and stiffly beaten whites are fully incorporated; no liquid egg or separate yellow or white pieces remain visible. After chilling, they give the cream its pale ivory-yellow colour and an airy, softly set, spoonable structure, not a baked or firm custard texture.

Chilled with the eggs into two thick layers of pale ivory-yellow cream, airy and creamy yet softly set, each roughly 1–1.5 cm thick. The surface is matte to lightly satin, with a few tiny soft mascarpone lumps and a gently levelled, unpiped top; it is dense yet aerated, neither runny nor grainy or split.

About 2–3 elongated finger biscuits per portion, originally roughly 8 x 2.5 cm, broken as needed into roughly 4–6 cm lengths and arranged in two layers. After their brief coffee dip and chilling they are soft, moist, spongy ladyfinger pieces, patchy light to medium coffee-brown, with darker soaked surfaces and pale golden-beige porous centres. They remain recognisable as separate biscuit strips rather than cake slices, crisp biscuits or mush.

Absorbed into the biscuit crumb, with no liquid pool or separate coffee layer in the glass. It creates the darker soaked surfaces and irregular coffee-brown patches, while less soaked centres remain pale golden-beige.

Fine, dry, matte, deep cocoa-brown powder, sifted over the cream just before serving in a continuous, slightly uneven dusting. It remains a thin powdery veil, not chocolate shavings, sauce or a wet glaze; pale cream may show only at the edge.
